bull_case: Flight heritage plus owned applications can deepen switching costs and cross-sell.
bear_case: SpaceX scale and defense-prime incumbency can cap pricing power, while acquisition breadth may add complexity rather than moat.
thesis: The moat is broadening from Electron launch heritage into vertically integrated mission capability. It is strengthening, but not yet a fully proven compounding ecosystem because Neutron and post-Iridium integration remain forward-looking.

evidence.claim: Rocket Lab launched 21 Electron missions in 2025.
Space Systems represented roughly two-thirds of FY2025 revenue.

counterevidence: Rocket Lab remains cash-flow negative on a standalone basis and the Iridium transaction materially increases integration, financing and dilution complexity.
unknowns: Neutron commercial readiness and launch economics
Long-run dilution cadence and owner FCF/share conversion
falsifiers: A major Neutron delay, persistent launch failures, failure to close/integrate Iridium, or continued double-digit share dilution without per-share FCF progress would weaken the thesis.

hard_veto_flags.rationale: Revenue, backlog, launch cadence and product breadth do not show persistent moat shrinkage.

next_checks: Neutron schedule, backlog conversion, post-close Iridium FCF, diluted share count, ATM usage

subscores.rationale: Flight heritage, launch integration, qualification and spacecraft program continuity create switching friction.
Vertical integration and growing installed flight heritage reinforce customer trust, but a classic network effect is still limited.
Electron, HASTE, Neutron, spacecraft/components and Iridium create multiple defenses against any one launch market becoming commoditized.

uncertainties.rationale: Rocket Lab remains in a high-investment, acquisition-heavy transition with large execution variance.
